messages.name: Pell Dunmore
messages.text:
Pell slows a step before the yard opens properly, letting Bram's shield take the lead and dropping half a pace behind Sefa's shoulder.

"Quarry's gone quiet like a tavern when the Fist walks in," he says, low, not taking his eyes off the man in the apron. "Tools down, cart half-loaded, no mule. Nobody knocks off for dinner mid-load. Either they ran, or they were told to."

He keeps his hands easy and visible, thumbs hooked in his belt, but his eyes work the yard the way they'd work a street before a job: the sheds, the spoil heaps, the lip of the terraces above the house, the ground around the lower cut — looking for anyone lying low, blood in the dust, a second line of smoke, footprints heading off in a hurry.

"Bram, you do the talking — you look like a man people hand things to. I'll stay back a bit and watch the sheds. Sefa, if he asks us in, don't go first."

Then, raising his voice just enough to carry across the yard, friendly and ordinary: "Morning! Maela Thorn sent us up from Beregost for the case. You'd be the warden?"

messages.name: Bram Halloway
messages.text:
“Quiet for a working quarry,” I murmur to Pell and Sefa.

I walk into the yard toward the house, shield resting low and sword sheathed, watching the sheds and lower cut for movement as I go. I stop a few paces short of the man, leaving his doorway clear.

“Morning. Bram Halloway. Maela Thorn sent us for her case of dye-salts. Are you the warden?”

I glance back at the abandoned cart. “Have we come at a bad time?”

messages.name: Sefa Marrin
messages.text:
Sefa slows at the edge of the spoil yard and lets the silence sit a moment. “No ring of iron. No mule in the traces.” She glances at Pell and Bram, voice low. “That’s either the warden or the reason he can’t come to us. I’d like the case in hand before we learn which.”

She calls toward the doorway, open hands raised no higher than her shoulders. “Well met. We’re from Maela Thorn’s shop in Beregost, sent to collect a sealed case before the coach leaves at sunset.” She stays where she is, waiting to see whether the man invites them closer.

scenes.narration:
Bram goes first across the yard, shield low and sword sheathed. Sefa stops at the edge of the spoil heaps with her hands open. Pell drops back half a pace behind her shoulder, and his eyes go to work.

The yard gives him nothing that looks like trouble. Nobody lies low behind the spoil heaps, and nothing moves along the lip of the terraces above the house. The doors of the three stone sheds are shut and the lifting frame hangs still. The only smoke is the grey thread from the chimney. There's no blood in the white dust, which shows everything. What it does show is boots, a lot of them, scuffed into a broad trampled band that runs from the lower cut to the cart track and down it, the way the three of them just came up. Last night's damp has crusted the prints. They don't drag and they don't scatter. Inside the band he can make out a mule's hooves, with one man's prints walking beside them. Near the lower cut the hammers and wedges lie in the dust. One sledge stands upright on its head against the cart wheel, handle up, the way a man stands a tool he wants seen.

Bram stops a few paces short of the doorway and leaves it clear. The man in the apron looks at him and at the sheathed sword, then past him to Sefa's raised hands and to Pell hanging back. He takes his time with each of them.

"Hale," he says at last. "Osric Hale. Warden." His voice is low and rough with dust. "Bad time." He jerks his chin at the empty cart. "Lads walked off yesterday at the noon bell. Three weeks, not a copper from the Gate. Can't say I'd have stayed."

He lets his arms drop from his chest, and one hand rests on the ring of keys.

"Case is here. Sealed, like she wants it." He looks at Bram, then at Sefa, because she was the one who said *before sunset*. "She paid for that salt, your Maela. Somebody took her money. Wasn't me, and it wasn't my men." He stops there, and nothing on his face moves. "Who'd she pay?"

He doesn't wait to watch them answer. He turns and goes back inside. He leaves the door open behind him, and the heat of a small fire comes out into the bright yard along with the smell of a kettle that has boiled too long. Through the doorway there's a plain table and a single chair, a shelf of ledgers, and an iron-bound box about the size of a loaf of bread on the floor by the hearth, right at his feet.

messages.name: Bram Halloway
messages.text:
I move to the threshold, staying where Pell and Sefa can see me, and keep my hands away from my weapons.

“She didn’t tell us who took payment. Hired us to collect a sealed case from you and carry it back. That’s all we were given.”

I nod toward the ledgers. “Ten years guarding wagons taught me that the man carrying the goods isn’t always the man holding the purse. Who owes your lads their wages?”

“Is there a receipt or a message we can take back with the case?”

messages.name: Pell Dunmore
messages.text:
Pell doesn't follow him in. He stays where the open door and the three sheds are all in his eye-line, and speaks just loud enough for Bram and Sefa.

"Tracks say he's telling the truth about the lads. Whole crew walked off down the track together, no running, no dragging, mule and one man with them. Crusted from last night's damp. And that sledge by the cart's been stood on its head — handle up. That's a message, not a man dropping his tools. Quarrymen's way of saying 'we're owed.'"

He nods at the doorway. "Case is on the floor by his boot, and his hand's on his keys. He's not stalling, he's bargaining. That question — 'who'd she pay?' — that's a man wondering if the coin went to the owners in the Gate while he and his crew went three weeks dry. He wants to know if Maela's one of them or one of us."

He steps a little to the side, so the sheds and the track behind them stay in view and nobody coming up from below would find his back turned.

"Bram, go in and answer him straight — we don't know who she paid, we're hired hands same as his lads, ninety gold between three of us and not a copper of it his quarry's. Sefa, stay in the doorway where I can see you. I'll keep the yard." A beat, quieter still: "And if he names a price for letting that box leave the floor, don't say yes before we've heard the number. There's a sunset on this."

scenes.narration:
Bram comes up to the threshold and stops where Pell and Sefa can still see him, with his hands well away from his belt. Inside, Osric Hale has his back to the fire. He hears Bram out without moving and doesn't interrupt. At *who owes your lads* his eyes go to the ledger shelf, and they stay there.

"Vandarren." He says it like the name of a bad well. "House in the Gate. Owns this hill on paper. Never seen one of them up here. Their factor takes the money. Man called Hask." He pulls a folded letter from between two ledgers and drops it open on the table where Bram can read it from the door. The hand is good, the paper better. *Wages to follow by the next coach.* It's dated five weeks back. "Next coach came. Wages didn't."

He looks at the case by his boot, then at Bram.

"Receipt I can write. Weight, seal, day it left. And what's owed. Fourteen men, three weeks. Fifty gold and some silver." He says the figure flat, the way a man reads a tally he has added more than once. "Your Maela paid somebody for that salt. You don't know who. She does. She writes it down, who and how much, and that paper goes to my lads at the Red Sheaf in Beregost. Tonight. Not up here to me. To them." He pauses. "One of you gives me a name on that, the case goes with you."

Out in the yard Pell keeps the sheds, the track and the doorway in his eye-line, and Sefa hasn't moved from the edge of the spoil heaps, her hands still open at her sides. Nothing comes up the cart track. Nothing moves along the terraces. The lowest of the three sheds sits right against the lower cut, with an iron bar dropped across its door from the outside. The white dust in front of it lies smooth. Yesterday's boots went past it on both sides, and none of them went in.

Osric takes a ledger down from the shelf and opens it on the table. He sets a bottle of ink beside it and begins to write, slowly, pressing hard. The kettle ticks on the hob. The case sits where it was, at his feet.

messages.name: Sefa Marrin
messages.text:
Sefa steps forward until she is just at the edge of the light from the doorway, still outside but close enough to be heard without raising her voice. She lowers her hands and meets Osric’s eyes.

“I’m Sefa Marrin. We’re hired for the day, same as your lads were hired for the stone. I don’t know who Maela Thorn paid, but I’ll promise you this: if that case leaves with us now, I’ll go to her shop the moment we’re back in Beregost, and I’ll see that she writes down who and how much, sealed and in her own hand. Then I’ll carry it to the Red Sheaf myself and put it into the hands of your men before the night’s over.”

She lets that settle, then adds, quieter but very steady, “If we don’t have the case to her by sunset, none of us are paid, and a woman who’s out a sale won’t write anything for anyone. You’d be trusting me, but it’s a trust with my pay behind it. I’d rather see fourteen men get what they’re owed than carry a sealed box for Vandarren and call it done.”

messages.name: Pell Dunmore
messages.text:
Pell doesn't go in. He comes as far as the door-post, where the yard is still at his shoulder, and speaks to Osric past Bram.

"Vandarren. Upper City, old money, patriar house — I know the gate they live behind, never been through it. And a factor named Hask who writes a good hand on good paper." He nods at the letter. "That's not a man short of coin. That's a man holding it."

He lets that sit, then: "Your price is cheap, Warden. You're asking for a piece of paper and a walk to the Red Sheaf, and I'm going past its door tonight either way. I'll carry it. Pell Dunmore, Lower City. Write that on your receipt if you want a name to curse if it doesn't arrive." A small shrug. "Whether Maela writes down who she paid is Maela's business, and we can't promise her hand for her. We can promise she's asked, in front of your lads, and that they hear the answer same time we do. That's what I'll give you, and I don't give more than I can carry."

Then, lighter, as if it were an afterthought — but his eyes are on Osric's face when he says it: "One thing, since we're writing things down. Lowest shed by the cut — bar across it from the outside, dust in front of it smooth as a tablecloth. Your lads walked round it both sides yesterday and nobody went near. Powder store? Or something you'd rather we didn't carry back to Beregost along with the salt?"

He keeps half his attention on the yard behind him while he waits for the answer, and the other half on how long Osric takes to give it.

messages.name: Bram Halloway
messages.text:
“Bram Halloway. Put that down.”

I glance back at my companions, then meet Hale’s eyes.

“I’ll ask Maela for a signed account of who she paid and how much, and take it to your lads at the Red Sheaf tonight. If she refuses, I’ll go there anyway and tell them so. I can give you my word on what I’ll do—not on what she’ll write.”

I nod toward his letter. “Let me copy Hask’s promise and its date to show her. Who should I ask for at the Sheaf?”

screens.Pell Dunmore:
Sefa moves up to where the light from the doorway ends, staying outside, and gives Osric her name. She tells him the three of you are hired for the day, just as his crew were hired to cut the stone. She pledges that if the case leaves with you, she will go to Maela Thorn's shop in Beregost, have Maela put in writing, sealed and in her own hand, who was paid and how much, and bring it to Osric's men at the Red Sheaf before the night is out. She adds that if the case isn't with Maela by sunset, none of you are paid, so her own wages stand behind the promise. She says she would sooner see fourteen men get their due than hand over a sealed case to Vandarren and consider the job finished.

Bram gives his name and offers much the same. He will ask Maela for a signed record of her payments and the sums, and bring it to the crew at the Red Sheaf this evening. If Maela refuses, he will still go and tell them so. He vows only what he himself will do, not what Maela will write. He asks to copy down Hask's promise with its date so he can show it to her, and asks whom to look for at the Sheaf.

Osric listens to all three of you with the pen gripped in his fist, and he doesn't look up until every one of you has finished. Then he writes, slowly, pressing hard, muttering each name as it goes down: Halloway, Marrin, Dunmore. He angles the ledger toward the door so you can read it: one case, sealed, Thorn's mark, seven pound and some, left Whitestone this day, and owed the crew, fourteen men, three weeks, fifty-two gold and six silver. Your three names stand beneath it in his heavy square hand.

He tells Sefa that with her pay behind it, you will walk fast. To you he says the price is not cheap to him. To Bram he says nothing at first. He pulls a clean leaf from the back of a ledger and pushes it across the table with the ink bottle and the Vandarren letter, setting the pen on top. "Copy it. Letter stays here." Then he answers Bram: ask at the Red Sheaf for Wat Pryor, the carter who took the mule. He is owed the most, so he will be the loudest.

Then you ask about the lowest shed by the cut. Osric's hand comes off the page and settles on his ring of keys. You watch his face and wait for his answer.

I don’t know who Maela Thorn paid, but I’ll promise you this: if that case leaves with us now, I’ll go to her shop the moment we’re back in Beregost, and I’ll see that she writes down who and how much, sealed and in her own hand. Then I’ll carry it to the Red Sheaf myself and put it into the hands of your men before the night’s over.”

She lets that settle, then adds, quieter but very steady, “If we don’t have the case to her by sunset, none of us are paid, and a woman who’s out a sale won’t write anything for anyone. You’d be trusting me, but it’s a trust with my pay behind it. I’d rather see fourteen men get what they’re owed than carry a sealed box for Vandarren and call it done.”

Pell Dunmore: Pell doesn't go in. He comes as far as the door-post, where the yard is still at his shoulder, and speaks to Osric past Bram.

"Vandarren. Upper City, old money, patriar house — I know the gate they live behind, never been through it. And a factor named Hask who writes a good hand on good paper." He nods at the letter. "That's not a man short of coin. That's a man holding it."

He lets that sit, then: "Your price is cheap, Warden. You're asking for a piece of paper and a walk to the Red Sheaf, and I'm going past its door tonight either way. I'll carry it. Pell Dunmore, Lower City. Write that on your receipt if you want a name to curse if it doesn't arrive." A small shrug. "Whether Maela writes down who she paid is Maela's business, and we can't promise her hand for her. We can promise she's asked, in front of your lads, and that they hear the answer same time we do. That's what I'll give you, and I don't give more than I can carry."

Then, lighter, as if it were an afterthought — but his eyes are on Osric's face when he says it: "One thing, since we're writing things down. Lowest shed by the cut — bar across it from the outside, dust in front of it smooth as a tablecloth. Your lads walked round it both sides yesterday and nobody went near. Powder store? Or something you'd rather we didn't carry back to Beregost along with the salt?"

He keeps half his attention on the yard behind him while he waits for the answer, and the other half on how long Osric takes to give it.

Bram Halloway: “Bram Halloway. Put that down.”

I glance back at my companions, then meet Hale’s eyes.

“I’ll ask Maela for a signed account of who she paid and how much, and take it to your lads at the Red Sheaf tonight. If she refuses, I’ll go there anyway and tell them so. I can give you my word on what I’ll do—not on what she’ll write.”

I nod toward his letter. “Let me copy Hask’s promise and its date to show her. Who should I ask for at the Sheaf?”

messages.name: Pell Dunmore
messages.text:
Pell takes the answer at face value, or at least lets it look that way. "Fair enough. Flooded seam's a flooded seam." He nods at the case. "Mind if I handle it? Only I'd rather know now if the seal's sound than have Maela tell me at sunset."

He steps in, lifts the case once by the handle to feel the weight against the seven-and-some on the ledger, turns it to the window light and looks at the wax on the hasp — whether it's one pour or two, whether the hasp's been worked under it — then sets it down again. He folds the receipt and tucks it inside his jerkin where the rain won't get it.

"Warden. We'll see Wat Pryor tonight, and your fifty-two and six goes on the table in front of him in writing, whatever Maela says to it." A short nod, the kind that closes a deal in the Lower City. "Bram, finish your copy and let's walk. We've eaten the morning."

Out in the yard, waiting for the others, he lets his glance pass over the barred shed once more — not to go near it, just to fix it in his head: the bar, the hinges, the dust — and then turns to the cart track. "Same way down we came up. The crew's tracks go that way, so if there's anyone on the road it'll be them, and they're the ones we're carrying good news to."

messages.name: Bram Halloway
messages.text:
I copy the letter carefully, including its date, and let the ink dry before folding it with the receipt and stowing both safely.

“Wat Pryor. Fifty-two gold, six silver. I’ll find him tonight.”

I check the case’s handle and fastening without disturbing the wax, then lift it, keeping my shield arm free.

“Thank you, Hale. Your kettle’s near dry.”

Outside, I pause beside Pell and Sefa. “Case and papers secured. Let’s get our wages earned while there’s daylight.” I keep my voice low. “Anything else we need to know before we take the road?”

messages.name: Sefa Marrin
messages.text:
Sefa steps just inside the threshold, enough to stand by the table but not further than that. She bends her head to look at the wax seal on the hasp — whole, with Thorn’s mark pressed clean — and then straightens.

“Fifty-two and six,” she says quietly, as if fixing the sum in her memory. “I’ll carry that number like a prayer until I’ve put it in Wat Pryor’s hand.”

She takes up the receipt, folds it once, and tucks it carefully inside her belt against the Book of Shadows, where it won’t be lost. She doesn’t reach for the case until Bram has finished his copy and the letter is back in Osric’s keeping. Then she lifts it carefully, finds it lighter than she expected, and holds it against her side with both hands.

“We’ll see Maela’s answer before dark,” she says to Osric, “and whatever she writes, someone will stand at the Red Sheaf tonight and say it true to Wat.” She looks to Bram, then out through the door to Pell. “I mean to keep my part of that promise.”

scenes.narration:
Pell takes the case by its handle and lifts it once. It weighs what the ledger says, seven pounds and a bit, and nothing inside it slides or knocks. He turns it to the light from the doorway. The wax over the hasp went on in one pour, with Thorn's mark pressed clean into it and no second skin or seam at the edges. The hasp under it hasn't been bent or worked. As far as a man who has opened a great many sealed things can tell, nobody has opened this one. He sets it back beside the receipt, then folds the receipt and puts it inside his jerkin.

Osric watches him do it and says nothing. When Pell promises the fifty-two and six will go on the table in front of Wat whatever Maela says, the warden nods once.

"Do that."

Bram sits on the corner of the table, since the room has only the one chair, and copies the letter slowly. He takes down the date, the good hand's *Wages to follow by the next coach* and the Vandarren name at the foot of it. Then he waits for the ink to dry. It takes a few minutes in that warm room. Osric doesn't hurry him. When Bram slides the letter back across the table along with the pen and the ink bottle, Osric puts the letter back between the same two ledgers it came from. Bram folds his copy and stows it. When Bram mentions the kettle, Osric looks at it as if he'd forgotten it was there. He lifts it off the hob with a corner of his apron and sets it on the hearthstone, where it hisses.

"Third time this morning."

By the time Sefa steps over the threshold, the receipt is already inside Pell's jerkin and Bram has the case on its handle in his sword hand, with his shield arm free. She bends over it to look at the wax all the same. When she says *fifty-two and six* and *like a prayer*, Osric looks at her for a long moment.

"Say it true, then. Wat can tell when it isn't."

That's all he has for her. He sits back in his one chair. He doesn't get up to see them off.

Out in the yard the sun has climbed higher and the white dust throws it back hard enough to make the eyes ache. Pell lets his glance cross the barred shed once more. The iron bar sits in two brackets bolted into the stone. The hinges are old, black and dry. The brackets aren't. Both of them have a bright line worn into the iron where the bar rides, the kind of shine that only comes from a bar being lifted out and dropped back again and again. Rust would have dulled that shine in a season. In front of the door the dust lies as smooth as before.

Then the cart track takes his eye. It runs down the way they came, along the lip of the lower cut, with the crew's trampled band of boot prints in it. Bram stands by him with the case, and Sefa comes out of the doorway into the glare. Behind them the warden's door stands open. Inside, the kettle has stopped ticking.

messages.name: Bram Halloway
messages.text:
“Aye. Same road back.”

I set off with Pell and Sefa along the crew’s tracks, carrying the case on the side away from the cut. Near the quarry edge I keep to the firm inner part of the track, watching for loose ground; farther on, I keep an eye on the road ahead.

“Let’s keep a steady pace. I’d rather reach Maela with time to talk than have her buyer loading the coach while we ask after Hask.”

messages.name: Sefa Marrin
messages.text:
Sefa blinks hard as the white glare meets her, then falls in with the others at the cart track. “Keep the case between us—not out front, not trailing,” she says. “If Wat Pryor or any of the crew are waiting down the road, they’d want the box, not a brawl. And if they’re not, we still want it in Maela’s hands before the sun slides.”

She settles the receipt against her belt, loops a thumb through her prayer beads, and leaves her right hand free near the Book of Shadows. Then she gives Pell a small, wry look. “You watch the bends ahead. I’ll watch our backs and the white dust behind us, in case Osric’s lads come to see what their warden gave away.”

messages.name: Pell Dunmore
messages.text:
Pell falls into step beside Bram and says nothing until the warden's door is behind the first spoil heap and the hut is out of earshot. Then, quiet, eyes on the track ahead:

"Shed's not shut three years. Brackets on that bar are worn bright where it rides — that's iron lifted out and dropped back week in, week out. A season of rust would've dulled it. He opens it. Regular. And he answered me about it like a man reading the weather, which is either the truth or a lot of practice."

He lets that settle a few paces.

"I'm not saying we go back. We've a box, a sunset, and three names in a ledger that says we walked out of here honest. A man barring his own shed on his own hill isn't our job, and I don't poke locks I'm not paid to poke." A glance at Sefa. "But I'd want it known between us. If something's wrong with the salt, or with Vandarren, or with Osric Hale, that shed's where I'd start looking — and I'd sooner start looking with the ninety in my pocket and Wat Pryor's lot behind me than alone on a hillside with a flooded seam under my feet."

He checks the sun, then the track. "Walk steady, not fast. Crew's tracks go all the way down; if they've camped short of town we'll pass them, and I'd rather pass fourteen angry quarrymen as the men bringing their tally than as three strangers with a Vandarren box." He unslings the shortbow as he goes, not strung for a fight, just within reach, and takes the outside of the track where he can see down the slope.

scenes.narration:
Bram keeps to the firm inner edge of the track with the case on his far side. Sefa walks half a step behind him and looks back up the white slope toward the warden's door. Pell takes the outside line along the lip of the lower cut, the unstrung bow in his hand, his eyes on the drop to his left and on the bend ahead.

They are forty paces past the last spoil heap when Pell's next step lands on ground that sounds wrong. It booms, like a boot on a floorboard. Then the crust of white dust under him folds inward, with a crack of old timber underneath it, and the track takes Pell Dunmore straight down.

He drops eight feet through dust, splinters and black water. His shoulder hits a ledge of stone on the way down, and he lands hard on his side in water that closes over his head, so cold it punches the breath out of him. He comes up coughing, with a split lip and a burning ache down his ribs where the ledge caught him. He's battered, but he's whole and he's breathing.

He isn't free, though. Something came down with him. A squared block of white stone, about the size of a sea-chest, slid off the ledge in the collapse and settled across his left leg below the knee. It pins the leg to the floor of the working. The water stands at his chest.

Daylight comes through the hole above in a ragged shaft, about four feet across, and in it Pell can see where he is. He's in a low chamber cut square into the hill, an old working with tool-scored walls. The far end goes off into dark water under a sagging roof. Crusts of crystal grow on the walls just above the waterline, rose-white and glittering like sugar on a cake. Somewhere a thin seep trickles in, steady, and the cold water moves against his chest with it. A tarred beam thicker than his arm, one of the old roof props, lies half-sunk against the wall within easy reach.

The block is not plain quarry stone. The face turned up toward the light has been dressed smooth, and cut into it, worn soft but deep, is a sunburst: a round face with straight rays running out to the edges. Around it runs a ring of small marks, notches, ticks and crossed strokes, too regular to be chisel slips. They're set close, like a row of writing in a hand nobody uses any more.

When Pell tries the leg, the stone answers with a bright, tearing pain. The block's underside isn't dressed like its face. It's jagged, and that edge has bitten into his shin and is sitting in the wound, pressing it shut. He can feel the blood moving under the stone, held there. The block is far too heavy for one man lying in water. And whoever shifts it is going to open that cut wide the moment it lifts. Anyone working on that stone will want healing ready in hand when it moves.

Up on the track, Bram is standing on the firm inner edge, six feet from a hole that wasn't there a breath ago. Fresh dust is still running in over its lip. The ground around the hole is grey under the white crust, where the rotten timber of an old roof shows through. Sefa is beside him. Looking down past the broken edges, they can both see Pell in the shaft of light below, chest-deep, with his head and shoulders up and the white block across his leg.

Back at the house, the door bangs. Osric Hale is coming down the slope at a heavy, rolling run, his keys clashing at his belt. He stops a long stride short of the grey ground and doesn't step onto it. He looks down into the hole, and for the first time today his face shows something plainly. messages.name: Sefa Marrin
messages.text:
Sefa doesn’t step toward the broken ground. She drops to one knee well back from the grey edge and pulls a loose wedge of chalk-stone from the track with a sharp tug. “Keep still down there, Pell—don’t turn your leg under that block.” Her free hand flares briefly like a lit wick, and the stone in her grip fills with soft white light. She tosses it, underhand, so it falls near the hole’s edge but not onto Pell: enough to light the water and the timber around him.

Then she holds out a hand to Bram. “Give me your arm. Lantern, steady his hands,” she murmurs, and a faint warmth runs from her fingers into his arm as the prayer takes.

She looks straight at Osric. “Rope. And planks or a timber laid flat to spread our weight if we have to work near him. Don’t walk on the grey ground. He’s chest-deep and pinned; we’ve minutes, not an hour.”

messages.name: Bram Halloway
messages.text:
I set the case well back on firm ground, shed my shield beside it, and pull out my rope.

“Pell, rope coming. Under your arms if you can—tell us what’s holding your leg. We won’t haul against it.”

I make a fixed loop wide enough for his shoulders and lower it toward him from the firm inner edge, keeping my weight back from the rotten timber.

“Sefa, help me hold him above water. Hale—fetch a long stout beam or a quarry lever. And tell us what else is down there.”

I brace to take the rope’s strain once Pell has it secured, without trying to wrench him free of the block.

scenes.narration:
Sefa kneels well back from the grey ground and works a loose wedge of chalk-stone out of the track. When she closes her hand on it, light runs into the stone like oil soaking a wick, and it glows a steady white in her palm. She tosses it underhand. It drops past the broken edge, clips a splinter of old timber and comes to rest on the ledge just above the waterline. From there it lights the whole low chamber.

From above it all looks harder and closer than the daylight let on. Black water fills the chamber wall to wall. The rose-white crystal glitters above the waterline in its crusts. The tarred prop lies half-sunk against the near wall, and the squared block lies across Pell's leg with its sunburst turned up to the light. Next to the ledge where the block came from, the chamber wall stops being tool-scored stone. A patch about the size of a cupboard door has been plastered over smooth, old and grey, with the edges feathered into the rock by someone who took care over it. The slide knocked a corner off, and behind the break there is darkness.

Sefa holds her hand out to Bram. When he gives her his arm she murmurs to the Lantern, and warmth goes from her fingers into his forearm and settles there like a coal held in a cupped hand. It is a short prayer, the kind that lasts for one push and not much longer, and she has to keep her mind on it while it lasts.

Bram moves fast. He sets the case down on firm ground well back from the cut and leans his shield against it. Then he shakes out his rope and ties a fixed loop wide enough to pass over a man's shoulders. He stays on the firm inner edge, plants his heels and lets the loop down over the broken lip. It goes through the shaft of light and settles on the water within easy reach of Pell's hands. The rope runs taut from Bram's fists to the hole, and his weight stays back where the ground is white and sound.

From where he kneels he can see the block properly, and what he sees he has seen before, on the Trade Way, under an overturned wagon. The block's underside is jagged. Its edge sits down in the shin, and in the light a thin pink thread curls up through the water from under the stone and drifts away with the seep. The stone is crushing the cut and holding it shut at the same time. As soon as the weight comes off, the leg will bleed all at once, and in cold water a man goes under fast from that. Whatever healing they mean to use has to be in someone's hand and ready the moment the block moves, not fetched afterward. Lifting it is not the hard part. With the stone the size of a sea-chest and that tarred beam lying right there for a lever, two people can shift it in a few minutes. One of them works the bar or the beam under the block's edge, and the other takes the weight on a rope.

Osric doesn't answer Sefa straight away. He is already moving. He goes at his heavy rolling run to the lifting frame and comes back dragging two long planks off its staging, with an iron pinch-bar as long as a man across his shoulder. He stays a full stride short of the grey ground. Leaning on the planks, he shoves them out one after the other over the rotten crust so they lie flat along the near side of the hole, reaching from firm ground to the broken lip. He drops the pinch-bar on the sound ground beside Bram's boot with a clang.

"Bar." He jerks his head at the hole and doesn't look away from it. "Prop's down there with him. Tarred. Won't rot." When Bram asks what else is down there, he takes a moment, and his eyes go across the glittering walls. "Old cuts. Run back under the hill. Roof's bad all the way." He stops. "Water comes in slow. Don't want anyone down there longer than it takes."

He doesn't step onto the planks. He stands at their landward end with one boot on each to hold them steady, and he watches the light on the water.

The seep goes on trickling in, and the water around the block barely moves with it.

 (Out of game: none of these needed a roll, and the turn already played them all: Light and Guidance are cantrips that just work, Sefa's words to Osric are plain talk he acted on, and lowering a fixed loop from firm ground is routine for Bram.)

The rope runs taut from your fists to the hole, and your weight stays back where the ground is white and sound. You ask Sefa to help hold him above water, tell Osric to fetch a long stout beam or a quarry lever, and ask what else is down there.

From where you kneel you can see the block properly, and what you see you have seen before, on the Trade Way, under an overturned wagon. The block's underside is jagged. Its edge sits down in the shin, and in the light a thin pink thread curls up through the water from under the stone and drifts away with the seep. The stone is crushing the cut and holding it shut at the same time. As soon as the weight comes off, the leg will bleed all at once, and in cold water a man goes under fast from that. Whatever healing you mean to use has to be in someone's hand and ready the moment the block moves, not fetched afterward. Lifting it is not the hard part. With the stone the size of a sea-chest and that tarred beam lying right there for a lever, two people can shift it in a few minutes. One of them works the bar or the beam under the block's edge, and the other takes the weight on a rope.

Osric doesn't answer straight away. He is already moving. He goes at his heavy rolling run to the lifting frame and comes back dragging two long planks off its staging, with an iron pinch-bar as long as a man across his shoulder. He stays a full stride short of the grey ground. Leaning on the planks, he shoves them out one after the other over the rotten crust so they lie flat along the near side of the hole, reaching from firm ground to the broken lip. He drops the pinch-bar on the sound ground beside your boot with a clang.

Don't want anyone down there longer than it takes."

He doesn't step onto the planks. He stands at their landward end with one boot on each to hold them steady, and he watches the light on the water.

The seep goes on trickling in, and the water around the block barely moves with it.

messages.name: Pell Dunmore
messages.text:
Pell spits water and blood and gets one hand on the ledge to hold himself steady against the pull of the seep. His voice comes up the shaft hoarse but level — the voice of a man who's been stuck in worse holes and knows panic drowns you faster than water.

"I'm alive. Leg's pinned under a block — big one, dressed stone, won't shift on its own. Water's at my chest and it's coming in slow. I've got a roof-prop within reach I can use for a lever, but I'm lying wrong for it; I need weight on the long end from someone who can stand."

He looks up at the three faces. "Bram. Rope's in my pack — I'm getting it off now and I'll tie it round the beam end so you can haul it up and feed yourself down. Shield off first, mail or no mail, you don't want to go in that water heavy. Sefa — the stone's edge is sitting *in* the cut; when it lifts, the leg opens. I'll have a potion in my hand, but I want your light ready the second after, not the second before. Don't come down until Bram's set."

He works the pack strap off his shoulder one-handed, gets the silk rope out, and starts a loop round the end of the tarred beam, teeth helping where fingers are numb.

Then, flatter, up at the warden, while his hands keep moving: "Hale. You said don't stay down here. I'm not planning on it. But say why. Is it the water, the roof, or what's growing on the walls? Because these pretty crystals look a lot like something a woman in Beregost would pay for by the case — and I'd like to know what I've been breathing before I do any more of it."

He gets one potion out of the satchel and palms it, cork under his thumb, and waits for rope and weight.

scenes.narration:
Pell's hand finds the ledge. The stone is slick, and under his fingers there's a grit that isn't quarry dust. It's crumbled plaster from the broken corner of the smooth grey patch beside him. Behind that corner the dark gives off air that's dry and still. It's the only dry thing down here.

He shrugs the pack strap off one-handed, and the cold makes it a fight. The silk rope comes out wet and stiff. The tarred prop lies half-sunk against the wall an arm's length away, as thick as his thigh and heavier than it looks. Getting the line around its end means working blind under the water, so he does it with his fingers, his teeth and an old habit. Round twice, a hitch, and he pulls it hard. The knot holds. The free end trails up the wall toward the light, ready for whoever takes it. Bram's loop is still on the water by his elbow, turning slowly in the seep.

The potion comes out of the satchel next. He holds it in his fist with his thumb on the cork, above the waterline. Below him the thin pink thread keeps curling up from under the stone.

Up at the lip, Osric Hale hears Pell's question through. He doesn't answer straight off. His hand goes to the ring of keys and stays there.

"Salt. Hers." He says it low, at the hole, not at anyone. "Grows where the wall's wet. Seam's full of it."

The seep goes on trickling for a while before he speaks again.

"Man drowned down there. Three years back. Four feet of water." His jaw works once. "Didn't fall. Didn't get pinned. Just went under."

He takes his hand off the keys and sets his boots back on the ends of the planks.

"Out first. Talk after."

The water lies flat and black around Pell's chest. It's a finger's width higher than it was when he landed.

messages.name: Bram Halloway
messages.text:
“That stone’s holding a bad cut shut,” I tell Sefa. “Have your healing ready before we shift it. Soon as his leg’s clear.”

“Pell, I’m coming down to work the lever. Leave the stone until we’re ready.”

Once Pell has the loop secured, I hand the rope to Hale. “Hold him steady from solid ground. When he’s free, you haul. Sefa, can you cover him from here?”

I leave my sword and pack beside the case, keeping my healer’s kit with me. Staying low on the planks to spread my weight, I work toward the opening and lower myself down as carefully as I can, using the iron bar if the tarred prop won’t serve. I want a firm purchase under the block before applying pressure.

“Everyone ready before we lift. No surprises.”

messages.name: Sefa Marrin
messages.text:
Sefa keeps her grip on Bram’s arm, the Lantern’s warmth still banked in it, and fixes her eyes on the rope as it settles. “Take the loop under your arms first, Pell, not in your hands. If the block shifts or the water rises faster, you want the rope doing the work, not your fingers.”

She doesn’t crawl onto a plank. She stays on sound ground, but she leans forward just enough to see past the broken lip. “When you’re clear, I’ll have light and healing ready. Until then, talk to me—can you feel your foot? Is the block on the leg or the whole shank?”

Her gaze flicks to Osric as he steadies the planks. “That sunburst slab didn’t come from any quarry face I know. Was that down there when you shut the low seam, or did someone set it after?” Her voice is calm, but she watches him closely, as if his answer might matter almost as much as the rope.

scenes.narration:
Bram says it plainly to Sefa: the stone is holding a bad cut shut, so the healing has to be in hand before it moves. Then he calls it down the hole to Pell. He turns to Osric and holds out the hempen line.

Osric looks at the rope for a moment, then takes it. He keeps both boots on the ends of the planks, wraps the line twice round his forearm and plants his heels in the white dust.

"Got it."

Bram sets his sword and pack down beside the case, keeps the healer's kit at his belt, and goes out onto the planks on his knees and then on his belly, spreading his weight the way a man crosses spring ice. The planks creak and give a little. Under them the grey crust ticks and settles, and a dribble of old timber-dust runs off the broken lip into the water. The planks hold. At the edge he turns, lets his legs down over the lip, hangs from his hands in his chain mail for a breath, and drops.

The water takes him to the belly, and it's cold enough to make his teeth set. The floor under his boots is stone, slick with something gritty that isn't quite sand. As he lands he feels Sefa's warmth thin out in his forearm and go, the way a coal dies when the hand around it opens. The prayer's minute has run out. Up on the lip, Sefa feels it slip loose from her too.

Down here the chalk-stone's light is hard and close. The rose-white crust glitters on every wall just above the waterline, and the sagging roof is low enough that Bram has to bow his head. He gets his hands on the block and reads it the way he'd read a wagon on its side. The high edge rests on a broken lump of the fallen ledge. On the wall side there's a gap three fingers wide between the block and the rubble, with good rock floor beneath it, and a loose chunk of the ledge lies right there to serve as a fulcrum. The tarred prop is long and stout, but in this low room there's no height to swing it, and the tar would slide in a man's grip. It won't work as a lever. Its end would make a good chock, though. The job is to get iron into that gap, lift the block a hand's breadth, jam the prop under it so it can't come back down, and draw the leg out while it's held. That takes one man on the bar and another on the leg or the rope. And healing has to be ready the moment the jagged edge comes up out of the shin.

messages.name: Pell Dunmore
messages.text:
Pell takes the warning the way he takes most warnings — as a reason to hurry, not to freeze. "Heard. Out first." He gets the free end of the rope coiled and flings it up the shaft toward the lip, hard enough to clear the dust.

"Bram, that's tied to the prop, not to me — don't haul it yet. Come down it. Shield and pack stay up top, mail you keep if you must, but you go slow and feet-first; there's a ledge about four feet down on my side, you can land on that and not in the water. Once you're on it, haul the prop up out of the wet and we'll set the thin end under this block's edge, heel on the ledge. You put your weight on the long end; I'll feel the stone come up and pull the leg. Sefa — you stay up there till it moves, then your light down to me, hard as you can give it. Hale, make yourself useful: a pick or a wedge from the cart, anything flat to chock under the block once it lifts so it doesn't come back down on us. Toss it, don't bring it."

While he waits, he keeps his free hand on the ledge, his head well clear of the water, and his eyes on the surface around him — not the crystals, the water, and the dark under the sagging roof where the seep is coming from. A man doesn't "just go under" in four feet of water unless something put him there or he'd already stopped breathing right. He slows his own breathing deliberately, shallow and through the nose, and keeps talking so the others can hear he's still clear-headed.

"One more thing, since I've nothing to do but notice. There's a patch of plaster by my shoulder, corner broken, dry air behind it — only dry thing down here. Somebody walled something up in this seam, and this block with the sunburst came from it. Not our business today." A grim half-smile up at the light. "But I'm putting it in the ledger with the shed."

scenes.narration:
Pell gets the wet silk coiled in his numb free hand and throws it up the shaft. The first throw is short. The coil opens against the broken lip and slithers back, raining dust onto the water around him. The second throw clears it. The rope goes over the edge and its end lands on the near plank by Osric's boots. Now the line runs taut and dripping from the hitch on the prop, up the wall and through the light.

Bram doesn't need to come down it. While Pell was talking, he dropped in over the lip in his mail, and the splash slapped water into Pell's face. Now he's on his feet a long stride away, belly-deep beside the block and bent under the low roof. The plan Pell called up the shaft was made for a man still up top.

From down here Pell can see what's wrong with the rest of the plan too. The roof sags low enough that Bram has to stoop. There isn't room to raise the prop out of the water, let alone swing its long end. The tar on it is slick under Pell's palm where he braces against it. The iron pinch-bar is up at the lip, sticking out over the edge of the near plank. Osric slid it out there before Pell's rope came up.

Osric hears Pell's request for a chock and doesn't move his feet. He keeps Bram's rope wrapped twice round one forearm and both boots on the plank ends.

"Got the line. Can't leave it." He looks at the black prop in the water. "That's your chock. Tar won't crush." He doesn't toss anything down.

Pell keeps his hand on the ledge and his head well up, breathes shallow through his nose, and watches the water instead of the walls. It shows him nothing. The seep comes out of the dark under the sagging roof in a thin, steady trickle with no current in it and no ripple that doesn't come from it, from his own body or from Bram's. Nothing moves in the black at the far end. The dry air from the broken plaster keeps drifting past his cheek, faint and dusty, smelling of nothing at all. The only thing working on him down here is the cold. His fingers are going clumsy, and his left foot has stopped answering him with anything but the ache in his shin.

When he mentions the plaster, Osric's eyes go to the grey patch by Pell's shoulder and stay there a moment. His jaw sets.

"Leave the wall."

He has nothing more to say about it. Rope in hand, he watches the water. It has crept up the block's dressed side again, and it's halfway now between the bottom of the sunburst and the bottom of its ring of marks.

messages.name: Bram Halloway
messages.text:
I take the pinch-bar from Osric and set its tip into the wall-side gap, with the loose stone as a fulcrum on the sound floor. I put the end of the tarred prop within reach to chock the block.

“Pell, can you wedge that prop under when I lift? Keep your fingers clear. If you can’t, say so.”

I look up. “Hale, take the slack, but don’t pull till his leg’s clear. Sefa—ready with the healing?”

Once everyone confirms they’re ready, I brace my feet and bear down steadily on the bar, aiming to raise the jagged edge just a hand’s breadth and hold it while Pell chocks it and frees his leg.

messages.name: Sefa Marrin
messages.text:
Sefa stays on sound ground and shifts a little along the firm white edge, not onto the planks, tilting her head to read the ring of marks through the broken lip where the light falls. Her lips move once, silently, and then she says clearly, “That’s not just masons’ marks. It’s writing. It says, *cut no further*—and further around, *that the rest be kept*. It’s a warning carved into the stone, not a decoration.”

She says it down into the hole, calm but firm. “So don’t chip at that plastered patch, and don’t widen anything down there. If the old cut was sealed on purpose, we don’t want to find out what was meant to stay kept.”

Then she looks at Bram. “Work the bar under the block on the side away from Pell’s leg, and lift slow. The moment it shifts, I’ll have healing light on him.” Her hand stays near the Book of Shadows, and her voice carries above the trickling seep. “Osric, keep the rope and the planks both steady. If the roof settles, we haul Bram first and Pell straight after.”

messages.name: Pell Dunmore
messages.text:
Pell abandons the plan without a wasted breath — a plan is just the last idea you hadn't thrown away yet.

"Right. Forget the prop, Bram, there's no roof to swing it under. Sefa — the pinch-bar, on the plank by Hale's boot. Toss it down to Bram, iron end first, into the water not onto us. Hale, keep that line, you're doing the right thing."

He gets his shoulder against the wall and his free hand flat on the dressed face of the block, feeling for the gap where the ledge meets its underside. "Bram — bar goes in here, under the near edge, this ledge for your heel. Short lever, so it's all your back. You don't need to lift it, you need to lift it an inch and hold it. I'll shove the prop's end under with my foot — tar won't crush, he's right about that — and then I pull the leg and you let it down on the wood, not on me."

He gets the potion cork loose with his teeth, holds the bottle above the water in his fist, and shifts the prop with his good foot until its end is nosed up against the block, ready to go under.

"Sefa, the moment you hear me say 'clear,' your light. Not before — if you spend it while the stone's still on me the cut just closes again under it." A hard breath through his nose. "On your count, Bram. Water's not waiting for mine."

scenes.narration:
Bram reaches up and takes the iron pinch-bar where it sticks out over the lip. Osric lets it go without a word. It's as long as a man is tall and heavy with cold. Bram ducks under the sagging roof with it and works the tip into the three-finger gap on the wall side, away from Pell's leg, just as Sefa calls down. He kicks the loose lump of fallen ledge into place on the sound floor under the bar for a fulcrum. With his other hand he hauls the tarred prop round by Pell's silk line until its blunt end lies against the block's flank. Pell's good foot finds it and noses it up to the edge, ready to go under. The bar is short in that low room, so this will be all back and no swing.

Up on the white edge, Sefa moves along the firm ground, still off the planks, until the light from the chalk-stone falls across the ring at a better angle. With Bram bent to the bar, his shoulders no longer hide the left side of the block. The marks settle into words for her the way they did before, square and cramped. *...here the white sleeps. Cut no further...* Then, further round, *...bring no fire to the white...* After that the ring dips toward the bottom of the block, and the water has covered that stretch. Black water lies over the last arc of marks, and her reading stops where it begins. The broken lip still cuts off the far side.

She says what she can read down the hole, plainly. Osric goes very still at the landward end of the planks. The rope stays wrapped twice round his forearm.

"*Fire*," he says. Nothing else. His eyes go to the crystals glittering on the wall, and he doesn't look away from them.

Pell has the cork out of the flask with his teeth. He holds the potion above the water in his fist and keeps his free hand flat on the sunburst, feeling for the moment the stone moves.

Bram counts. On the last word he bears down.

The bar bends a little. The fulcrum stone grinds on the floor. For a long breath the block does nothing, and then it comes up. It rises slowly, a finger's width, then two, then a hand's breadth, the dressed face tilting toward the light, and water slops off its edge. Bram holds it there with his back locked and his teeth set. Pell drives the prop's end under with his good foot. It goes in, black and slick, and Bram lets the block down onto it a hair's breadth at a time. The wood groans and takes the weight. The tar doesn't crush.

Pell pulls his leg out.

The jagged edge comes up out of the shin, and the water around his leg turns dark at once. The blood isn't a pink thread now. It comes up thick and fast, and Pell's face goes grey in the light. The cold had been holding most of the pain back, and now all of it arrives.

Sefa's hand comes off the Book of Shadows, and the light leaves it.

It drops down the shaft like warm lamplight poured from a jug and lands on Pell's leg under the water. The bleeding stops. The torn edges of the shin pull together under the light, ragged and angry but closed. Warmth climbs the leg past the knee, and the grey goes out of his face. It's a full, clean measure of the Lantern's light, the best one die of it can give. He's still cold, still bruised along the ribs, still sore with a cut lip, but he's not bleeding out into the water now, and he's free.

The block sits on the tarred prop a hand's breadth off the floor where Pell's leg used to be.

Then the broken corner of the plaster beside Pell's shoulder starts to glow.

It isn't bright. It's the dull warm light of a coal behind a screen, coming through the crack from the dark inside. Pell feels it on his cheek as heat, the only warm air in the room, and it comes from the same place as that dry, still breath. It lasts while the last of Sefa's light fades off the water. Then it sinks away slowly, the way an ember goes down.

Up on the edge, Osric Hale has seen it. He doesn't move his feet off the planks, and he doesn't let go of the rope. His hand goes to the ring of keys at his belt and closes on it hard enough that the iron clinks.

Down in the working the seep goes on trickling in. The water has crept up the block's tilted face and now laps the lowest of the sunburst's rays.

 (Out of game: I didn't roll any of the three because none of them was uncertain. The setup already says two people with a lever and a chock can shift the block in a few minutes, and holding a rope from firm ground is routine work for Osric. All three actions happened as the scene describes them.)

Pell has the cork out of the flask with his teeth. He holds the potion above the water in his fist and keeps his free hand flat on the sunburst, feeling for the moment the stone moves.

Bram counts. On the last word he bears down.

The bar bends a little. The fulcrum stone grinds on the floor. For a long breath the block does nothing, and then it comes up. It rises slowly, a finger's width, then two, then a hand's breadth, the dressed face tilting toward the light, and water slops off its edge. Bram holds it there with his back locked and his teeth set. Pell drives the prop's end under with his good foot. It goes in, black and slick, and Bram lets the block down onto it a hair's breadth at a time. The wood groans and takes the weight. The tar doesn't crush.

Pell pulls his leg out.

The jagged edge comes up out of the shin, and the water around his leg turns dark at once. The blood isn't a pink thread now. It comes up thick and fast, and Pell's face goes grey in the light. The cold had been holding most of the pain back, and now all of it arrives.

Sefa's hand comes off the Book of Shadows, and the light leaves it.

It drops down the shaft like warm lamplight poured from a jug and lands on Pell's leg under the water. The bleeding stops. The torn edges of the shin pull together under the light, ragged and angry but closed. Warmth climbs the leg past the knee, and the grey goes out of his face. It's a full, clean measure of the Lantern's light, the best one die of it can give. He's still cold, still bruised along the ribs, still sore with a cut lip, but he's not bleeding out into the water now, and he's free.

The block sits on the tarred prop a hand's breadth off the floor where Pell's leg used to be.

Then the broken corner of the plaster beside Pell's shoulder starts to glow.

It isn't bright. It's the dull warm light of a coal behind a screen, coming through the crack from the dark inside. Pell feels it on his cheek as heat, the only warm air in the room, and it comes from the same place as that dry, still breath. It lasts while the last of Sefa's light fades off the water. Then it sinks away slowly, the way an ember goes down.

Up on the edge, Osric Hale has seen it. He doesn't move his feet off the planks, and he doesn't let go of the rope. His hand goes to the ring of keys at his belt and closes on it hard enough that the iron clinks.

Down in the working the seep goes on trickling in. The water has crept up the block's tilted face and now laps the lowest of the sunburst's rays.

messages.name: Sefa Marrin
messages.text:
Sefa puts a hand on Osric’s shoulder and murmurs, “Lantern, steady his hands,” letting a brief warmth run into his arms for the next pull. Then she raises her voice down the hole.

“Pell — loop under both arms, high as it’ll go. Don’t hold your whole weight on the bad leg, and don’t let go. Bram, leave the block where it is and lift him from below if you can. Haul steady on three, not a snatch.”

She shifts back onto sound ground, sits her weight into the rope’s tail if it slips, and keeps her eyes on Pell’s face rather than the glowing plaster. “And if that ember-light comes again, don’t stare into it. It’s not for us.”

messages.name: Pell Dunmore
messages.text:
Pell gets the cork back in the potion with his thumb and shoves it into the satchel. Not spent. A man who's just been handed free healing doesn't waste the paid kind.

"Sefa — no more light down here. Not a cantrip, not a glow. Whatever's behind that plaster just woke up when yours touched the water, and the writing says *no fire to the white*. I'd rather it went back to sleep without learning our names."

He doesn't look at the crack again. He turns his back on it, deliberately, and gets his good foot on the ledge.

"Bram, you're the heavy one and you're in mail — you take Hale's line, now, before the water's at your neck. I'll come up the wall; I've climbed worse in the dark with a Fist patrol under me." He tests his left leg against the stone — it takes weight, grudging and sore, but it takes it — and reaches up for the first tool-score in the rock. "My rope stays on the prop. Costs me a good silk line, but if that block comes off the wood when we're gone I'd sooner it didn't have anything of mine tangled round it. Hale — once Bram's on the planks, you can take your hand off those keys. We're leaving your wall alone. All of us." A flat glance up at the warden's face. "But a man drowned in four feet of water with a warm wall for company, and you've kept a shed barred and bright over this seam for three years. That goes in the ledger too. You can tell it to me walking, or you can tell it to Wat Pryor tonight when I tell him why I'm limping."

He climbs — hands and knees and the scored walls, the way he'd take a chimney breast — up toward the ragged four-foot square of daylight, and doesn't stop to look down at what's glowing or not glowing behind him.

messages.name: Bram Halloway
messages.text:
“Pell’s free. Haul him up, Hale—steady.”

I help guide Pell beneath the opening, keeping his injured leg clear of the block and leaving the prop undisturbed.

“Something behind that plaster answered the healing. Leave it alone. We’re getting out.”

Once Pell is safely up, I ask them to lower the loop for me. I secure it under my arms and climb toward the planked lip with their help, using the sound rock where I can and keeping off the rotten timbers.

scenes.narration:
Osric feels Sefa's hand settle on his shoulder. Her murmured prayer goes into his arms like warmth from a hearth. He doesn't look round. He takes the hempen line in both fists and sets his heels deeper in the white dust. Sefa steps back onto sound ground behind him and takes up the rope's tail across her hip, ready to sit her weight into it. Her eyes stay on the hole and on the faces in it.

Down below, Pell pushes the cork back into the flask with his thumb and pushes the potion down into the satchel, still unspent. He says what he has to say about the light. Then he turns his back on the cracked plaster and finds the ledge with his good foot. The chalk-stone keeps burning where it lies, steady and white, so the working is still lit. The plaster corner gives back nothing. It's grey and dark and only plaster, and the dry air still drifts out past the break.

Bram comes up beside him, belly-deep, and gets a hand under Pell's elbow to steady him at the wall. He keeps Pell's left leg clear of the block and doesn't touch the prop. "Something behind that plaster answered the healing. Leave it alone. We're getting out."

The left leg takes Pell's weight when he tries it. It's sore and the new skin across the shin pulls tight, but it holds. He doesn't need the loop. The old tool-scores in the wall are as good as a ladder to a man who learned on chimney breasts above the Wide. His fingers are numb, but they find the cuts one after another, and he goes up the wall fast, the way he always climbs. Water streams off him. At the top he reaches past the rotten edge, gets both hands flat on the near plank, and rolls out onto it and off it again onto firm white ground. He's soaked to the collar and shaking with cold, and he's out. Behind him the silk rope still runs down over the lip, tied to the black prop under the block, and it stays there.

Osric watched him come up the whole way. He doesn't answer Pell's last words about Tobin and the shed. "Up first," he says. "Both."

The loop goes back down to Bram. He works it over his head and under both arms, snugs it high, and calls it. Sefa counts three and Osric hauls, steady, without snatching, and the warmth in his arms makes the pull smooth. Bram climbs with the rope taking his weight and the scored rock under his boots. His chain mail sheds water like a shaken dog. At the lip he keeps off the grey crust and comes over flat onto the planks. They bow under him and creak, and a spill of old timber-dust runs down into the water. The planks hold. He crawls the length of them to the white ground, where his shield, sword and pack lie by the case.

The two of them stand in the glare, dripping. Down in the hole the pinch-bar is still wedged in its gap, and the block sits on its tarred chock with the sunburst a hand's breadth higher than it was this morning. The black water has started on the lowest rays.

Osric lets the line go slack and unwraps it from his forearm. It has left a red welt there. He coils it slowly into rough loops and holds it out to Bram. Then he looks at Pell, and this time he keeps looking.

"Tobin Reed." He says it as if he hasn't said it aloud for a while. "Cutter. Good one. Low seam was stone then. Salt was just the muck on the wet walls." His jaw works. "Went down alone one evening. Clear the pump. Found him at first light. Face down. Four feet of water." A pause. "Wrote *drink* in the book. Tobin didn't drink."

He looks down the slope at the barred shed by the lower cut.

"Shed goes through. Back under the hill to the wet walls. Since her orders started I go in. Scrape the salt. Fill the case. Come out." His hand starts toward the keys and stops halfway. "Said shut. Wasn't. Never stay long. Never came this far along." He jerks his head at the hole and the grey plaster under it. "Never saw that wall. Didn't know it was there."

Then he stops, and it's plain he's said all he means to say on the open track. He stands with his empty hands at his sides, looking at the four of them and the hole. Behind him the house door is still open. The sun is a little past its height, and in the bright yard the wet footprints Pell and Bram left are already drying white.

 (Out of game, one line each:)

1) Sefa's warmth in Osric's arms is Guidance, a cantrip. It just works and needs no roll. It went into his haul on Bram's rope.
2) Sefa's directions are plain talk, so there was nothing to roll. Pell chose to climb instead of taking the loop, so her "haul steady on three" went to lifting Bram, and it went smoothly.
3) Pell's player wrote that he re-corked the potion and kept it, so he didn't drink it and there's nothing to roll. All three potions are still in the satchel.
4) Pell's climb didn't need a roll: eight feet of tool-scored wall is routine for a roof-runner with Second-Story Work, so he made it to the top as narrated.

"Bram, you're the heavy one and you're in mail — you take Hale's line, now, before the water's at your neck. I'll come up the wall; I've climbed worse in the dark with a Fist patrol under me." I help guide Pell beneath the opening, keeping his injured leg clear of the block and leaving the prop undisturbed.

“Something behind that plaster answered the healing. Leave it alone. We’re getting out.”

Your narration:
<<<
Osric feels Sefa's hand settle on his shoulder. Her murmured prayer goes into his arms like warmth from a hearth. He doesn't look round. He takes the hempen line in both fists and sets his heels deeper in the white dust. Sefa steps back onto sound ground behind him and takes up the rope's tail across her hip, ready to sit her weight into it. Her eyes stay on the hole and on the faces in it.

Down below, Pell pushes the cork back into the flask with his thumb and pushes the potion down into the satchel, still unspent. He says what he has to say about the light. Then he turns his back on the cracked plaster and finds the ledge with his good foot. The chalk-stone keeps burning where it lies, steady and white, so the working is still lit. The plaster corner gives back nothing. It's grey and dark and only plaster, and the dry air still drifts out past the break.

Bram comes up beside him, belly-deep, and gets a hand under Pell's elbow to steady him at the wall. He keeps Pell's left leg clear of the block and doesn't touch the prop. "Something behind that plaster answered the healing. Leave it alone. We're getting out."

The left leg takes Pell's weight when he tries it. It's sore and the new skin across the shin pulls tight, but it holds. He doesn't need the loop. The old tool-scores in the wall are as good as a ladder to a man who learned on chimney breasts above the Wide. His fingers are numb, but they find the cuts one after another, and he goes up the wall fast, the way he always climbs. Water streams off him. At the top he reaches past the rotten edge, gets both hands flat on the near plank, and rolls out onto it and off it again onto firm white ground. He's soaked to the collar and shaking with cold, and he's out. Behind him the silk rope still runs down over the lip, tied to the black prop under the block, and it stays there.

Osric watched him come up the whole way. He doesn't answer Pell's last words about Tobin and the shed. "Up first," he says. "Both."

The loop goes back down to Bram. He works it over his head and under both arms, snugs it high, and calls it. Sefa counts three and Osric hauls, steady, without snatching, and the warmth in his arms makes the pull smooth. Bram climbs with the rope taking his weight and the scored rock under his boots. His chain mail sheds water like a shaken dog. At the lip he keeps off the grey crust and comes over flat onto the planks. They bow under him and creak, and a spill of old timber-dust runs down into the water. The planks hold. He crawls the length of them to the white ground, where his shield, sword and pack lie by the case.

The two of them stand in the glare, dripping. Down in the hole the pinch-bar is still wedged in its gap, and the block sits on its tarred chock with the sunburst a hand's breadth higher than it was this morning. The black water has started on the lowest rays.

Osric lets the line go slack and unwraps it from his forearm. It has left a red welt there. He coils it slowly into rough loops and holds it out to Bram. Then he looks at Pell, and this time he keeps looking.

"Tobin Reed." He says it as if he hasn't said it aloud for a while. "Cutter. Good one. Low seam was stone then. Salt was just the muck on the wet walls." His jaw works. "Went down alone one evening. Clear the pump. Found him at first light. Face down. Four feet of water." A pause. "Wrote *drink* in the book. Tobin didn't drink."

He looks down the slope at the barred shed by the lower cut.

"Shed goes through. Back under the hill to the wet walls. Since her orders started I go in. Scrape the salt. Fill the case. Come out." His hand starts toward the keys and stops halfway. "Said shut. Wasn't. Never stay long. Never came this far along." He jerks his head at the hole and the grey plaster under it. "Never saw that wall. Didn't know it was there."

Then he stops, and it's plain he's said all he means to say on the open track. He stands with his empty hands at his sides, looking at the four of them and the hole. Behind him the house door is still open. The sun is a little past its height, and in the bright yard the wet footprints Pell and Bram left are already drying white.

messages.name: Pell Dunmore
messages.text:
Pell wrings the water out of his sleeves one at a time, then his hair, and says nothing while Osric talks. When the warden stops, he nods once — the nod of a man filing a thing away, not forgiving it.

"That's more than you gave me at the door. I'll take it." He stamps the left foot once on the firm ground, winces, and decides it'll walk. "Here's where I've got to, Hale, and you can tell me if I'm wrong. Three years back a good cutter goes under in water he could've stood up in, with a warm wall ten feet off that nobody knew was there. Somebody wrote *drink* so nobody'd ask. Then a woman in Beregost starts paying for the pretty salt off the same wet walls, and a house in the Gate takes her coin and stops paying your men. And you kept going in. Alone. Never stayed long." He glances at the hole, not the plaster. "I'd say your luck's been better than Tobin's and I'd not lean on it again. Bar the shed. Leave it barred. Whatever's behind that wall likes light and heat, and the salt grows on the same walls it breathes on. I don't know what that makes the salt. Neither does Maela. I mean to ask her."

He turns to the others. "Bram, case. Sefa, you've the receipt and the sum; keep them dry, I'm not a safe place for paper right now. We go, and we go now — I've got half a day of road, wet boots, and a lip that'll close by Beregost if I stop talking." A short breath. "Walk the inside of the track, all of us, against the cut wall, single file. If the seam runs under the track it runs under the outside edge, and I've met it."

He slings the unstrung bow, picks up his pack, and starts down — limping on the first dozen steps and less after that — keeping to the wall side. Over his shoulder, to Osric: "Wat Pryor gets his fifty-two and six on the table tonight. And Tobin Reed's name goes next to it. You can decide what you want said about the rest before we come back up this hill — because somebody will."

messages.name: Bram Halloway
messages.text:
I take the rope back. “Thank you for the haul.”

I recover my sword, shield and pack, then look at the sealed case without lifting it yet.

“Hale—is what’s in that box the same white stuff on those walls? What did Maela tell you about handling it—fire, heat, keeping it dry?”

I glance toward the broken track. “Nobody else should walk over that. Mark the approach from sound ground before another cart comes through.”

To Pell and Sefa, quietly: “We need Maela’s answers, but I won’t carry this into a busy shop without warning her what we found. Pell, how’s the leg for walking?”

messages.name: Sefa Marrin
messages.text:
Sefa doesn’t move from solid ground. She reaches toward the hole, and a ghostly hand—pale as lamplight, no warmer than a breath—dips over the lip and closes around the chalk-stone. It lifts the stone back into daylight and sets it in her palm. She holds it a moment, then speaks a quiet word, and the light in it goes out like a pinched wick. She drops the grey stone beside the case.

Then she looks at Osric and doesn’t look away.

“You said ‘since her orders started.’ I’m not carrying that case one step down the track until you tell me whose orders. Maela Thorn’s? And I need to know if what’s sealed inside is salt scraped off the wet walls there—from a place carved with *cut no further* and *bring no fire to the white*. Because people who took the trouble to write that were afraid of something still down there.”

She glances once at Pell, shivering-cold and dripping, and at Bram with his mail still dark with water. “We saw light in that wall answer a healing. If Maela sent us to fetch that without telling us what it was, then the promise we made her isn’t the only one that matters.”

scenes.narration:
Pell wrings out his sleeves one at a time while Osric talks, then his hair. Water spatters into the white dust and turns it grey for a moment. When the warden finishes, Pell nods once and has his say. Osric hears all of it. At *Bar the shed* his eyes go down the slope to the iron bar on its bright brackets.

"Bar stays down." A pause. "Till somebody tells me what it is." When Pell gets to Wat and the fifty-two and six and Tobin's name beside it, Osric's jaw works once. "Say his name. Rest's mine to say."

Pell is already moving. He stamps the left foot on firm ground, takes the wince, and goes down the track hugging the cut wall, single file with nobody behind him yet. The new skin on his shin pulls on the first dozen steps. After that it pulls less, though the limp doesn't go away completely. His boots squelch on the stone, and the sun is already drying the shoulders of his jerkin to a pale crust.

Bram takes the coiled rope from Osric's hands. "Thank you for the haul." Osric only shrugs and rubs the red welt on his forearm. Bram picks up his sword, belts it on, gets his shield back on his arm and shoulders his pack. Then he stands over the sealed case and looks at it without lifting it.

He asks his questions. Osric answers them in the order they came.

"Same." He nods at the hole. "Pink off the wet walls. Not the white stone. Scrape it, fill her case, seal it. Her stamp's on my shelf." He shifts his weight. "Keep it dry. Keep it shut. That's all she ever wrote me." He stops, then adds, "Never said fire. Nobody did."

He looks at the broken lip, where the dust is still trickling in, and seems to hear the last part only now.

"Nobody did till you," he says to Sefa.

Then he turns to the track. "Stakes off the frame. Rope across, both ends. Before dark." He says it like a thing already on his list, but it hadn't been until Bram said it.

Sefa stays on sound ground and reaches toward the hole. A pale hand, faint as lamplight, slips over the broken lip, goes down through the shaft of sun and closes on the glowing chalk-stone on the ledge. It brings the stone up past the rotten timber and sets it in her palm. She says a quiet word. The light goes out of the stone like a pinched wick, and she drops it, grey and ordinary again, beside the case. Below, the working goes dark except for the ragged square of daylight on the black water. Nothing else down there gives off any light.

Then she faces Osric and puts it to him plainly, without looking away.

Osric doesn't look away either. That takes him a moment.

"Hers. Maela Thorn's." He says the name the way he said *Vandarren*, flat, as if reading it off a tally. "Letter on the coach. Since the thaw. A case a month. Some months two." His hand moves toward the keys and stops halfway, the way it did on the track. "Same walls. Same wet. Never this far along. Didn't know the sun was down there, or the writing."

He looks at the grey stone she dropped, and then at the case beside it.

"Didn't know what I was scraping." His voice goes lower still. "Don't now."

That is all he says about it. He doesn't tell her not to carry the case, and he doesn't tell her to. Whatever promise she means beyond Maela's, he leaves to her. He turns and walks heavily toward the lifting frame, where a stack of old staging stakes leans against the upright. Behind him the house door still stands open on the cold kettle and the shelf of ledgers.

Down the track Pell has reached the first bend, a lone dark figure against the cut wall, leaving wet prints on the white stone. Bram stands over the case with his shield on his arm. Sefa stands beside him, the receipt dry in her belt against the Book of Shadows. It is a little past noon. Down at the lower cut, the barred shed sits in its smooth dust.

Over his shoulder, to Osric: "Wat Pryor gets his fifty-two and six on the table tonight. And Tobin Reed's name goes next to it. You can decide what you want said about the rest before we come back up this hill — because somebody will."

Bram Halloway: I take the rope back. “Thank you for the haul.”

I recover my sword, shield and pack, then look at the sealed case without lifting it yet.

“Hale—is what’s in that box the same white stuff on those walls? What did Maela tell you about handling it—fire, heat, keeping it dry?”

I glance toward the broken track. “Nobody else should walk over that. Mark the approach from sound ground before another cart comes through.”

To Pell and Sefa, quietly: “We need Maela’s answers, but I won’t carry this into a busy shop without warning her what we found. Pell, how’s the leg for walking?”

Sefa Marrin: Sefa doesn’t move from solid ground. She reaches toward the hole, and a ghostly hand—pale as lamplight, no warmer than a breath—dips over the lip and closes around the chalk-stone. It lifts the stone back into daylight and sets it in her palm. She holds it a moment, then speaks a quiet word, and the light in it goes out like a pinched wick. She drops the grey stone beside the case.

Then she looks at Osric and doesn’t look away.

“You said ‘since her orders started.’ I’m not carrying that case one step down the track until you tell me whose orders. Maela Thorn’s? And I need to know if what’s sealed inside is salt scraped off the wet walls there—from a place carved with *cut no further* and *bring no fire to the white*. Because people who took the trouble to write that were afraid of something still down there.”

She glances once at Pell, shivering-cold and dripping, and at Bram with his mail still dark with water. “We saw light in that wall answer a healing. If Maela sent us to fetch that without telling us what it was, then the promise we made her isn’t the only one that matters.”

He looks at the broken lip, where the dust is still trickling in, and seems to hear the last part only now.

"Nobody did till you," he says to Sefa.

Then he turns to the track. "Stakes off the frame. Rope across, both ends. Before dark." He says it like a thing already on his list, but it hadn't been until Bram said it.
